I remember a few years ago when almost all of the gaming journos were grading games partially on their graphics, or photo-realism. Nowadays you can still find sites that do this, despite time and time again we have so many games that have proven that graphics do not necessarily enhance the experience unless they are going for a more realistic feel or immersive effect. Okami is still one of the most beautiful games I have ever played (beautiful in many ways) but does not have anywhere near cutting edge graphics, nor at the time did it have cutting edge graphics.

So the question is what should games be graded on? * Gameplay * Story * Style/Art Design (as a sub for graphics)

What is your criteria for what makes a good game?
Discussion: How should games be graded?

Criteria used by popular sites like IGN and Gamespot (such as graphics, music, and the rest) are fine with me , but the primary grading value that has always held most importance to me, has been what was/is my experience like?

I don't think "gameplay experience" and the usual criteria used by reviewers are mutually exclusive BTW. Great music, as in Jeremy Soule's Skyrim soundtrack, enhanced my experience greatly. Awesome graphics (I have a lot more to say about my definition of 'awesome graphics' BTW) can also make for a better experience, for example.

Example to illustrate my point: I think my best gaming experience ever, was Chronotrigger. Played in on the SNES in 1999. I have never reached the peak of that experience, although games like The Elder Scrolls, the Fallout series have come close. Even though, by today's standards, the graphics are not so hot (they were at the time), the feeling, the ambience, the total immersion is what makes me grade the game the way I do.

A self-criticism: Judging a game by "how I experienced it at the time" is rather subjective, and doesn't give any attempted sense at putative objectivity, I guess. Be that as it may, my experience of the game (influenced by many factors as it is) is my primary criterion.

TL;DR - how one experiences the game trumps the usual criteria IMO.

PS. I wrote this while rather giddily drunk. Not sure how I'll feel about it in the morning.

I like when a review talks about how the game fits in with others in its genre, or even why it doesn't. Saying "You will love this if you enjoyed x" is very useful, as is "If you're looking for experience y, this is not your thing". Scores are meaningless - comparisons are much more useful.

On a scale of 1 - Zelda this is about a 9.

If I ran a game reviews website or column, this is what my grading system would look like:

  1. Kill it with fire. Anyone involved in its making who has a modicum of self-respect and respect would be very ashamed by this bile that they've spewed at the audience. This should never have seen the light of day.
  2. Very flawed. Here and there you can catch a glimpse of what could have been, but otherwise, this would not be my first recommendation to anyone. It seems like something went terribly wrong during development.
  3. Fun but did not reach its full potential. Depending on what you're in the mood for, this could be a lot of fun or a big disappointment. I genuinely hope the developers fare better in their next endeavour.
  4. A very enjoyable experience, no regrets. If you want your time well spent, play this! Great job, developers.
  5. Put this game on your bucket list. This game is a shining example of the craft and a historically and culturally significant work that must be preserved for future generations.

I wish reviewers would stop dividing their grades according to various aspects of the game. The people who do this have no serious interest in said aspects and thus can offer no serious criticism. Whatever seems "cutting-edge" they'll slobber over and call it a milestone in the craft. This Gamasutra post by Blake Reynolds (scroll down to the part about King of Fighters XIII) shows a good example of what happens when someone who doesn't give a damn about animation grades animation.
